sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.caveat: NIST records AI RMF revision work in progress in 2026.
material_points: AI risk management is lifecycle-wide and sociotechnical, with risks emerging from technical systems, human behavior, organizational context, and interactions.

Trustworthiness characteristics include valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed.
The Core organizes work into GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. GOVERN is cross-cutting across the other functions.
Risk measurement includes uncertainty. Inability to measure a risk precisely does not establish that risk as high or low.
AI actors should have explicit responsibilities, and verification and validation benefit from separation from model building and use.

sources.title: NIST AI RMF Playbook
sources.caveat: The Playbook is voluntary guidance, not a checklist, and is expected to evolve with the AI RMF.
material_points: The Playbook supplies suggested actions aligned to AI RMF subcategories, not a mandatory sequence.
Governance should define roles, responsibilities, chains of command, risk tolerance, monitoring, auditing, review, change management, and incident response.
Policies should connect AI governance with existing organizational governance and risk controls and should document testing and validation processes.
Risk management activity should be proportional to context, impact, likelihood, and organizational risk tolerance.
Documentation and transparency support accountability and make risk-management ownership inspectable.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
sources.caveat: The profile describes risks and suggested actions for generative AI and anticipates future revisions as evidence evolves.
material_points: The profile emphasizes four primary generative-AI considerations: Governance, Content Provenance, Pre-deployment Testing, and Incident Disclosure.
Generative-AI risks can arise across lifecycle stages and at model, application, and ecosystem levels.
Confabulation is a named risk: confidently stated erroneous or false content can mislead users.
Human-AI configuration risks include inappropriate anthropomorphism, automation bias, over-reliance, algorithmic aversion, and emotional entanglement.
Information integrity, data privacy, information security, harmful bias, and component integration require explicit risk treatment.
Some generative-AI risks remain uncertain because measurement science, system visibility, and empirical evidence are incomplete.

sources.title: ISO 42001 Implementation Checklist: A Practical Guide for Responsible AI Governance
material_points: This item is secondary implementation guidance and must not be represented as the normative ISO/IEC 42001 standard.

sources.title: NIST AI 600-1 Initial Public Draft
material_points: This historical draft is withdrawn and may be used only to demonstrate source lifecycle and supersession. It cannot be presented as current guidance.

scout_operating_constraints: Role or competence does not create authority.
Learning-path activation, VE lifecycle activation, capability grant, and task authorization are separate controls.
Scout may use only the supplied evidence packet for SCOUT-R001.
Scout may not recommend or perform authority expansion as an outcome of this assignment.
Scout must state uncertainty and missing or contradictory evidence rather than fill gaps with plausible claims.
Secondary guidance must not be represented as normative text.
Withdrawn material must remain visibly withdrawn and linked to its known successor.
Provider execution is local Ollama only and must remain zero paid cost.
required_synthesis_topics: GOVERN MAP MEASURE MANAGE as continuous controls
